title: Looking inside files
objectives: Read and search files with `cat`, `head` and `grep`.
Count lines with `wc -l`, and send output into a file with `>`.
Join two commands with a pipe, `|`.

screens.prose:
You only want Apple's rows from a small price file. A command called `grep` searches a file line by line for some text:

```sh
$ grep AAPL prices.csv
```
screens.question: Tap the lines you expect it to print.

hints.text: Which lines contain the text AAPL?
Each of these lines has AAPL in it.

feedback.correct: grep prints the three lines that contain AAPL.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every line that contains AAPL, and nothing else.

byKey.header: The header line has no AAPL in it. grep prints only the lines that contain the text.
byKey.r0c0: The header line has no AAPL in it, so grep skips it.
byKey.r2c0: That is a Microsoft line. It does not contain AAPL.
byKey.r4c0: That is a Microsoft line. It does not contain AAPL.
byKey.r6c0: That is a Microsoft line. It does not contain AAPL.

explain.text: grep printed the three lines containing AAPL, in the order they appear in the file. The header was dropped because it does not contain AAPL. The file itself is unchanged: grep only reads.

screens.prose:
grep does not know about columns. It looks for the text anywhere in each line. Try a piece of a date instead of a ticker:

```sh
$ grep 03-04 prices.csv
```
screens.question: Tap the lines this prints.

hints.text: Which lines contain the characters 03-04 somewhere?
Both rows from 4 March contain it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for 03-04 anywhere in each line.

byKey.one: You stopped at the Apple line. The Microsoft line from the same day contains 03-04 too.
byKey.one-b: You picked only the Microsoft line. The Apple line from the same day contains 03-04 too.

explain.text: grep matched 03-04 inside the date, so both rows from 4 March came out. It would also match 03-04 in a price or a name. Pick search text that can only appear where you mean it.

screens.prose: To print a whole file, use `cat prices.csv`. A big file floods the screen, though. `head` prints only the start. Here is the output of `head spx.csv`, a file of 2,517 lines of daily S&P 500 closes.
screens.question: How many lines did `head` print?

hints.text: Count the lines in the output, top to bottom.
The header is a line too.
One header line plus nine price lines.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every line of output, the header included.

byKey.all: That is the whole file, which cat would print. head stops early.
byKey.no-header: You left out the header. head counts every line, and the header is the first.

explain.text: head printed 10 lines, the header and nine days, then stopped. That is enough to see the columns and the date format. To scroll through a long file page by page, `less spx.csv` opens it; press q to quit.

screens.prose:
`wc -l` counts the lines in a file. The name is short for word count, and the `-l` asks for lines only. Back to the small file:

```sh
$ wc -l prices.csv
```
screens.question: What number does it print?

hints.text: wc counts lines, not rows of prices.
Is the header a line?
One header line plus six price lines.

feedback.correct: Seven lines: one header and six rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every line in the file.

byKey.rows: You left out the header. wc does not know it is special; it is still a line.
byKey.days: You counted trading days. wc counts lines, and each day has two.

explain.text: wc prints `7 prices.csv`: seven lines, then the file name. The header is one of them. So the file holds 7 − 1 = 6 price rows.

screens.prose:
So far every output went to the screen. The `>` sign sends it into a file instead. Nothing appears on screen:

```sh
$ grep AAPL prices.csv > aapl.csv
```
screens.question: Tap the lines that end up in aapl.csv.

hints.text: What would grep have printed on the screen?
These are the lines grep prints.
The file gets exactly what would have gone to the screen.

feedback.correct: aapl.csv holds the three AAPL lines, and no header.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The file receives exactly what grep would have printed.

byKey.header: You kept the header. grep never printed it, because it has no AAPL, so it is not in aapl.csv either.
byKey.r0c0: You kept the header. grep never printed it, so it is not in aapl.csv either.

explain.text: `>` caught grep's output and wrote it to aapl.csv. The header did not contain AAPL, so the new file has none. A spreadsheet would read the first price row as column names: that is the edge case to remember.

screens.prose:
The bar `|` is a **pipe**. It feeds one command's output straight into the next command, with no file in between:

```sh
$ grep AAPL prices.csv | wc -l
```
screens.question: What number does this print?

hints.text: What does wc receive: the file, or grep's output?
grep's output is these three lines.
wc counts the lines it receives: three.

feedback.correct: wc counted the three lines grep passed it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. wc only sees what grep sends it.

byKey.file: You counted the whole file. After a pipe, wc sees only grep's output.
byKey.header: You added the header. grep dropped it, so wc never sees it.

explain.text: grep picked three lines and the pipe handed them to wc. wc counted 3. Reading left to right, each command works on what the one before produced.

screens.prose:
You want one file holding both tickers' rows. You run:

```sh
$ grep AAPL prices.csv > picks.csv
$ grep MSFT prices.csv > picks.csv
$ wc -l picks.csv
```
screens.question: How many lines are in picks.csv?

hints.text: What happens to what was already in picks.csv when the second command runs?
These are the lines the second grep writes.
`>` empties the file before writing. The AAPL lines are wiped and replaced.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what `>` does to a file that already exists.

byKey.append: You expected `>` to add to the file. It empties the file first, so the AAPL lines were lost.
byKey.file: picks.csv never held the whole file, and the header was never in it.
byKey.none: The second grep wrote three lines after emptying the file. It is not empty.

explain.text: Each `>` starts the file afresh, so the second command wiped the AAPL lines. To add to the end of a file, use `>>` instead. The second line should have been `grep MSFT prices.csv >> picks.csv`.

screens.prose:
Every command so far reads lines and prints lines. That is why they snap together:

```sh
$ cat prices.csv        # all of it
$ head prices.csv       # first 10 lines
$ grep AAPL prices.csv  # lines with AAPL
$ grep AAPL prices.csv | wc -l
$ grep AAPL prices.csv > a.csv
$ grep MSFT prices.csv >> a.csv
```

A pipe passes output to a command. `>` writes it to a file, replacing it, and `>>` adds to the end.
screens.question: Which command saves the number of AAPL rows into count.txt?

options.why: The first `>` sends grep's output to a file named wc. Use a pipe to pass output to a command.
A pipe needs a command on its right. count.txt is a file, so the shell cannot run it.
You put the counting first. Commands run left to right, so wc would have nothing to count.

hints.text: Which sign passes output to a command, and which to a file?
First grep picks the lines, then a pipe passes them to wc, then `>` saves the number.

feedback.correct: Pick, pipe to count, then save.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A pipe feeds a command; `>` feeds a file.

explain.text: grep picks, `|` passes to wc, and `>` writes wc's number into count.txt. A pipe always has a command on its right. A `>` always has a file on its right.

screens.prose:
Before a backtest, you check how much history you have. spx.csv holds daily S&P 500 closes, one header line then one line per trading day.

```sh
$ wc -l spx.csv
2517 spx.csv
```
screens.question: How many trading days does the file cover?

hints.text: wc counted every line. Is every line a day?
This line is not a day.
Take the header away: 2517 − 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the header line off the count.

byKey.lines: You kept the header in the count. It is a line, but not a trading day.
byKey.years: That is roughly the number of years. The question asks for days.

explain.text: 2517 lines minus one header line leaves 2516 days. At about 252 trading days a year, that is close to ten years. One `wc -l` told you that without opening the file.

ideas: `cat` prints a whole file, `head` the first 10 lines, and `less` lets you scroll.
`grep` keeps the lines that contain some text, and `wc -l` counts lines, header included.
A pipe `|` feeds output to a command; `>` writes it to a file, replacing what was there.

formula.name: A first pipeline
formula.note: Read left to right: pick the lines, then count them.

summary.trap: `>` empties the file before writing. Use `>>` to add to the end.

quiz.prose: A file of tick data has two million lines. You want to scroll through it and quit when you are done.
quiz.question: Which command fits?

options.why: cat prints all two million lines at once. You cannot scroll back through most of them.
head shows the first 10 lines and stops. You cannot scroll further.

feedback.correct: less lets you page through and quit with q.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which command lets you scroll?

explain.text: less shows one screen at a time. Space goes down a page, and q quits back to the prompt.

quiz.prose:
prices.csv has 7 lines: a header and six rows. You run:

```sh
$ head prices.csv
```
quiz.question: How many lines does it print?

feedback.correct: A short file comes out whole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. head prints at most 10 lines.

byKey.ten: head prints up to 10 lines. This file only has 7, so it cannot invent more.
byKey.rows: head does not skip the header. It prints every line, up to 10.

explain.text: head prints the first 10 lines, or the whole file if it is shorter. Here that is all 7.

quiz.prose:
prices.csv holds the tickers in capitals, such as AAPL. You run:

```sh
$ grep aapl prices.csv
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.text: Nothing: no line contains aapl in lower case

options.why: You expected grep to ignore case. It matches the letters exactly as typed.
Finding nothing is not an error. grep just prints no lines.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare aapl with AAPL letter by letter.

explain.text: grep treats a and A as different characters. No line contains aapl, so nothing prints. The next lesson shows the option that ignores case.

quiz.prose:
Using the same prices.csv as in the lesson, you run:

```sh
$ grep 2024-03-05 prices.csv | grep MSFT
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: The second grep only keeps lines containing MSFT, so the Apple line is dropped.
The second grep only sees what the first passed on: the two lines from 5 March.

feedback.correct: Each grep narrows the lines further.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The second grep only sees the first one's output.

explain.text: The first grep keeps the two lines from 5 March. The pipe passes them on, and the second grep keeps the MSFT one.
